$comment: One regex list for the information-not-prose rule, read by prose.py. Patterns use syntax shared by JavaScript RegExp and Python re, and compile case-insensitive and multi-line. URLs are replaced by the token <url> before every scan, so a caption in front of a link can be seen. Scope flags: reply = the Stop hook applies it to chat replies; answer = text written on the user's behalf, such as email, form answers and replies; copy = product copy, such as landing pages, posts, captions and listings. A pattern may carry `requires` (a case-sensitive regex the sentence around the hit must also match), `unless` (a case-sensitive regex; when it matches that sentence the hit is dropped) and `min_words` (the sentence must carry at least this many words). The reply subset is kept to two patterns on purpose, because a guard that fires on ordinary replies gets switched off. Family 5 is scoped to answer and copy only for the same reason.
rule: INFORMATION, NOT PROSE. Before a sentence, ask who reads it and what they need from it. Write that. One fact per sentence: subject, verb, object, for example "You pay 25 percent of what the state grants." Use the reader's words and the product's own words. Never use a metaphor for the product, a coined noun, a label or caption in place of a sentence ("A four-minute tour of the product:"), or a noun phrase standing for a clause ("25 percent of relief granted"). A link is introduced by a sentence: "Here is a demo video: <link>". A money figure sits in a clause that says who pays whom: "You pay 25 percent of what the state grants, and nothing if we find nothing." A length limit is met by dropping a fact, never by deleting the subject or verb from a fact. No rhythm, no parallel triplets, no scene-setting, no "the X that Y" constructions, and no analogy unless a standard asks for one.
copy_rule: INFORMATION, NOT PROSE. Product copy states what the product does, what the reader gets and what the reader pays, in plain sentences with a subject and a verb. Use the product's own words, never a metaphor for the product ("under the hood", "secret sauce", "the magic"). A link follows a sentence ("Here is a demo video:"), never a caption ("A four-minute tour of the product:"). A percent or dollar figure sits in a clause with a payer and a verb ("You pay 25 percent of what the state grants"), never a bare noun phrase ("25 percent of relief granted"). A comma-chained list of noun phrases is not a sentence. A name or tagline is the plain noun ("four ranking sites"), not a noun with a clause hung off it. A length limit is met by dropping a fact, never by deleting a subject or a verb.

1.name: caption-for-a-link
1.title: CAPTION FOR A LINK
1.what: a noun phrase ending in a colon in front of a link, in place of a sentence that says what the link is

2.name: figure-without-payer
2.title: FIGURE WITHOUT A PAYER
2.what: a percent or dollar figure about money with no clause saying who pays or gets it

3.name: product-metaphor
3.title: METAPHOR FOR THE PRODUCT
3.what: a metaphor or coined name standing in for the product or one of its parts in outward copy

4.name: label-not-sentence
4.title: LABEL IN PLACE OF A SENTENCE
4.what: a noun phrase ending in a colon alone on a line, followed by prose or a link instead of a list

5.name: modifier-tail
5.title: MODIFIER TAIL ON A NAME
5.what: a naming fragment (a tagline, theme, headline or card line) with a relative clause or a participial phrase hung off the noun instead of just saying the plain noun

patterns.fix: write a sentence that says what the link is: Here is a demo video: <link>
put the figure in a clause with a payer and a verb: You pay 25 percent of what the state grants.
use the product's own words: name the part and say what it does
write the sentence the label stands for: Here is a demo video: <link>, or The state deadline is thirty days.
say the plain noun and stop: "four ranking sites", not "four boards, recounted every night"
say the plain noun and stop: "four ranking sites", not "four rankings nobody can buy their way onto"
